cross_tool_domains.attrition: Not assessable — Secondary single-country institutional case study synthesizing published cross-sectional surveys, scientific water-quality studies, and historical accounts with no primary cohort or participant follow-up.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern — Mentions historical infrastructure decay and debt from the 1970s-1980s, rapid urbanisation (from ~30% to >40% between 1990 and 2008), population/tourism/industrial demand growth, and bi-directional neighbourhood-income poverty, but uses no analytical or empirical strategy to disentangle these confounders from commercialisation or the 2005-2011 AVRL management contract.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Weak to moderate — Clearly maps PPP contractual forms (Table 1) and institutional restructuring (GWSC to GWCL in 1998, CWSA rural decoupling, PURC creation in 1997, AVRL management contract 2005-2011, GUWCL in 2011), but relies on secondary accounts rather than primary legal/contractual instruments, inconsistently cites the PURC enabling statute as both Act 538 (1997) and Act 578 on the same page (PDF Page 9, p. 1142), and conflates the implemented management contract with affermage in the concluding critique (PDF Page 9, p. 1142).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate to high concern — Establishes a clear multidimensional distinction between wide coverage and deep access (quality, reliability, cost, equitable distribution) using cited secondary metrics, but relies uncritically on heterogeneous secondary sources (including operator web pages, unpublished theses, and news portals) without auditing primary measurement validity or sample denominators.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate — Strong conceptual disaggregation of urban water outcomes across MDG coverage, microbial/chemical contamination, continuity and per-capita daily volume (litres/day), official tariff versus tanker-market pricing and household expenditure shares, and wealth-quintile/neighbourhood connection equity, but entirely dependent on secondary studies whose primary measurement procedures and sampling frames are not verified.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: High concern — No pre-specified protocol, literature search strategy, or source-inclusion rules; narrative assembly of secondary statistics and illustrative examples creates substantial risk of selective reporting aligned with the paper's critique of market-oriented water reform.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern — Purposive choice of Ghana as an illustrative national case is explicitly justified, but there is no documented search strategy or selection protocol governing which secondary surveys, scientific studies, dissertations, and media reports within Ghana were included or excluded.

domain_ratings.justification: Cites the Public Utilities Regulatory Commission Act, Act 538, 1997, PURC (2005) Urban Water Tariff Policy, National Urban Policy (2010), and UN General Comment No. 15 (2002), but exhibits internal legal/institutional inaccuracies: on PDF Page 9 (p. 1142) it cites Act 538, 1997 and four sentences later refers to the same statutory mandate as Act 578 without explanation; it also documents on PDF Page 6 (p. 1139) that Ghana abandoned affermage for a management contract with AVRL, yet on PDF Page 9 (p. 1142) repeatedly describes Ghana's implemented PPP with AVRL as affermage. Relies primarily on secondary literature rather than primary statutory or contractual texts.

overall_narrative_summary: Obeng-Odoom (2012) is a single-country political-economy and institutional-historical case study of urban water governance in Ghana (1957-2011) that synthesizes secondary histories, official statistics, scientific water-quality studies, and statutory/regulatory provisions without primary fieldwork, a comparator arm, or a systematic review search protocol. Appraised under the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework (as a structured non-validated judgment rather than a numeric score), the paper demonstrates strong jurisdictional specificity (D2), strong conceptual outcome definition distinguishing MDG coverage ("wide access") from quality, reliability, affordability, and distributional equity ("deep access") (D4), and strong political-economy institutional contextualisation of GWSC/GWCL restructuring, donor conditionality, civil society contestation, CWSA decoupling, and PURC-GWCL-AVRL regulatory asymmetries (D10), alongside adequate PPP exposure classification (D3) and secondary metric reporting (D7). However, methodological rigour for empirical and causal inference is severely constrained by the absence of a documented literature search or source-selection protocol (D5, D6, D11), lack of counterfactual causal identification or confounding adjustment separating the 2005-2011 AVRL management contract from long-standing infrastructure deficits and rapid urban growth (D8, D9), absence of methodological reflexivity (D13), and weak legal/institutional citation precision on p. 1142—where the PURC statute is cited first as Act 538 (1997) and four sentences later as Act 578, and where AVRL's arrangement is repeatedly referred to as affermage despite p. 1139 documenting that affermage was abandoned in favour of a management contract (D1).
overall_rating: Structured non-validated judgment: High methodological concern for causal/empirical inference (strong conceptual outcome framing, jurisdictional specificity, and institutional context; adequate exposure classification and secondary measurement reporting; weak legal citation precision, sampling/selection transparency, causal identification, confounding control, replication potential, and reflexivity; coding not assessable)
study_design_identified: Single-country institutional and political-economy historical case study synthesizing secondary survey, water-quality, and statutory/regulatory sources (no primary empirical data collection or systematic literature search)
where_found_summary: Case framing and aims on PDF Page 3 (p. 1136, Introduction); institutional and PPP history on PDF Pages 4-6 (pp. 1137-1139, Modern history of urban water provision in Ghana, including Table 1); secondary empirical synthesis on coverage, quality, reliability, cost, and equity on PDF Pages 6-8 (pp. 1139-1141, Access to water) and Note 2 on PDF Page 10 (p. 1143); statutory discussion of PURC (Act 538 / Act 578) and policy conclusions on PDF Pages 8-10 (pp. 1141-1143, Lessons, implications, and concluding remarks); bibliography and author note on PDF Pages 10-13 (pp. 1143-1146). No dedicated Methods section is present.
why_tool_chosen: The paper explicitly frames itself as a single-country institutional-historical case study of urban water governance and access in Ghana (1957-2011), tracing public utility restructuring (GWSC to GWCL), PPP contract selection (AVRL 2005-2011 management contract), and statutory regulation (PURC Act 538, 1997) alongside secondary empirical evidence. It fits none of the six conventional empirical checklists: there is no randomization (RoB 2), no comparator arm or quasi-experimental design (single-case histories without a comparator cannot be assigned to ROBINS-I), no primary cross-sectional or cohort dataset analysed (JBI), no primary qualitative fieldwork/interviews (CASP/MMAT), and no systematic search protocol (AMSTAR 2 is prohibited for non-systematic narrative reviews). The Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework directly matches this institutional/legal-historical case study design while capturing its secondary-source selection, confounding, and statutory accuracy limitations.
